US jobs: 165,000 positions created in October, more than double expectations, and the Fed keeps a rate hike in view

On Friday, November 6, the Bureau of Labor Statistics announced 165,000 jobs created in the United States in October, versus roughly 59,000 to 65,000 expected, and unemployment back down to 4.1%. Wall Street ended mixed: the Nasdaq rebounded 1.09% after the previous day's plunge [1][2][3].

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the US economy created 165,000 jobs in October. Economists had expected about 59,000 according to CNBC, 65,000 according to other sources: the figure is more than twice the consensus [1][2].
The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, versus 4.2% expected and 4.2% in September. A broader measure of underemployment, which also counts involuntary part-time workers, rose by 0.3 points to 7.9% [1].

Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% over the month and 3.1% over the year. September's figures were revised up: 60,000 jobs instead of the 29,000 initially reported, or 84,000 more jobs than estimated over the two months combined [1].
Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs, health care kept hiring, and manufacturing gained 19,000 jobs [1][2].

On Wall Street, the session was split: the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.09% to 24,579.42 points, the S&P 500 rose 0.31% to 7,376.86 points, while the Dow Jones fell 0.46% to 51,285.73 points, according to AFP [3].
The tech rebound remained timid after the Nasdaq's worst session since April 2025 on Thursday. US Treasury yields rose after the report, which weighed on part of the market [3].

Key takeaway: a strong jobs number is not always good news for the stock market. When the US economy hires more than expected, the central bank (the Fed) has less reason to ease its policy, and some analysts even see an argument for raising rates again in December [2][3].

The context explains this reading. Since the war in Iran, energy prices have pushed inflation back up, and the Fed faces a delicate choice: support jobs or curb prices. A solid labor market gives it room to pick the second option, at the risk of making credit more expensive for households and businesses [2].

The report is also a good sign for growth: jobs created in September and October exceeded forecasts, which for now rules out the scenario of an economic stall. But a single release does not make a trend, and revisions to the figures are frequent [1].

For the rest of the world, the Fed's decision matters: higher US rates draw capital toward the dollar and can weaken currencies and the debts of emerging countries, as seen this week with the Brazilian real [3].

If you have a variable-rate mortgage or plan to borrow, the path of US rates influences that of European rates, even though the ECB decides on its own. A stronger dollar also makes oil, which is priced in dollars, more expensive, and so the pump too. This report changes nothing in your daily life overnight, but it pushes back the idea of a quick rate cut.

Iran: Trump says a decision on new strikes or a deal will come “soon”, and calls the emir of Qatar

On Thursday, November 5, Donald Trump said a decision on new strikes against Iran or on a deal would be made soon. He also called the emir of Qatar, mediator on the Hormuz issue, while Tehran considers the US response insufficient and one more tanker was attacked this week [1][2].

In the Oval Office, Donald Trump said Iran was “largely destroyed” and that it would take more than twenty years to rebuild. He added that he might have to “destroy the rest”, without ruling out new strikes, despite his party's defeat in the midterm elections [1].

According to Axios, cited by several outlets, a US official says the US military command for the region (CENTCOM) is preparing major operations and is only waiting for the order from Washington. Fox News reports that Trump convened his national security team on Thursday on resuming operations [1][3].

A US official confirmed to CBS that Trump called the emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, to discuss efforts to end the war. Iran, for its part, has stepped up its diplomacy, with Russia and the United Arab Emirates [1][2].

On the Iranian side, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council judged Washington's response to fall short of expectations, and the Foreign Ministry said “the next step” was up to Trump [1].

Tehran says it is ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days, versus seven in its initial plan presented in September via Qatar, but on condition that its demands are met. Brent was worth about $106 on November 2, versus about $70 before the war, according to AFP [4].

US signals remain contradictory: earlier in the week, Trump told the Financial Times that Washington had no immediate plan to resume strikes, and a US strike had targeted an Iranian anti-aircraft facility on Tuesday, November 3 [1][3].

Key takeaway: we are at a tipping point, and both outcomes, a deal or resumed strikes, have direct consequences for fuel and energy prices in Europe. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a large share of Gulf oil and gas passes, remains the crux of the issue [4].

Qatar is the main channel: Doha speaks to both sides every day and is pushing for an agreement between Iran and Oman on transit conditions, a step seen as a prerequisite to resuming talks between Washington and Tehran. Trump's call to the emir shows the diplomatic route is not closed [2][4].

Trump's statements also move markets: Brent lost about 13% this week, mostly on hopes of diplomatic progress. Resumed strikes would quickly reverse that move, with Eurasia Group citing $110 to $125 a barrel in case of escalation [5].

Some uncertainty remains: part of the information comes from anonymous US sources, and opposing signals have circulated a few days apart. The safest approach is to read these announcements as negotiating positions, not as decisions already taken.

Gasoline and diesel prices in France follow oil with a lag of a few days: resumed strikes could cancel last week's decline, while a deal could extend it. This also weighs on heating bills and on inflation, and therefore on ECB decisions.

Kyiv in the dark: Dnieper bridges targeted by Russia, and Zelensky and Mayor Klitschko blame each other

On Friday, November 6, Russian strikes plunged Kyiv into darkness, with unprecedented power and water outages, according to Reuters. President Volodymyr Zelensky and Mayor Vitali Klitschko are trading blame over insufficient preparation, as Moscow targets the Dnieper bridges for the first time [1][2].

According to Reuters, Volodymyr Zelensky and Vitali Klitschko traded new accusations on Friday over the capital's lack of preparation for Russian strikes, which caused power and water outages on an unprecedented scale [1].

Zelensky described the situation as “extremely serious” and suggested the city administration bore part of the responsibility. It is the worst energy situation the country has known, according to his remarks reported by Reuters [1].

The strikes knocked out three DTEK thermal power plants, the country's largest private electricity producer, and forced emergency outages in Kyiv, in the Kyiv region and in the Dnipropetrovsk region [3]. The outages also repeatedly interrupted the metro [1].

Kyiv's bridges over the Dnieper are being attacked for the first time in nearly five years of war. In October, two days of assaults had already closed, fully or partly, three of the city's six road bridges, according to France 24 [1][4].

The North Bridge and the South Bridge carry tens of thousands of residents from one bank to the other every day; their closure creates massive traffic jams in the capital, according to the Kyiv Independent [5].

In his evening address, Zelensky said he had intelligence that Russia is preparing a new attack on energy, the Dnieper bridges and civilian infrastructure; Ukraine lacks air defense systems to shoot down fast missiles and drones [1][5].

Key takeaway: the war is now being fought over the infrastructure that daily life depends on, electricity, water, bridges, as winter approaches. Striking the capital's bridges aims to isolate the two banks, slow the delivery of aid and wear down the population's morale [1][5].

The quarrel between Zelensky and Klitschko is longstanding. Reuters recalls that elections are banned in wartime in Ukraine: both men therefore remain in office beyond their terms, which fuels the cross-accusations over responsibility for the outages [1].

The shortage of anti-missile systems remains the weak point: without systems able to intercept fast ballistic missiles, no protection of power plants or bridges is complete. Zelensky highlights this shortage in his appeals to his partners [1][5].
Four and a half years of war have already worn down the power grid: each plant hit reduces the country's winter generation margin a little more.

For a French reader, the effect is indirect but real: the longer the war lasts and the more it hits Ukrainian energy infrastructure, the more demand for financial and military aid from Europe rises, and that weighs on national budgets. The number of Ukrainian refugees in Europe could also grow if winter is harsh.

The Bank of England raises its rate to 4%, its first hike since August 2023, and sees inflation approaching 5%

On Thursday, November 5, the Bank of England raised its key rate by 0.25 points to 4%, by 8 votes to 1. It cites the energy surge linked to the war in the Middle East and forecasts inflation close to 5% in mid-2027, versus a 2% target [1][2][3].
The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8 to 1 for a 0.25-point rise in the key rate, to 4%. The ninth vote, from Catherine Mann, called for a 0.5-point rise [1][3].

It is the first hike since August 2023, after a long series of cuts. The bank justifies its decision by the rise in global energy prices, aggravated by the conflict in the Middle East, and wants to limit “second-round effects”, meaning contagion to other prices and to wages [1][4].

Its new forecasts are markedly bleaker: inflation is expected to approach 5% around mid-2027, versus 3.5% estimated in September. Boursorama mentions a worse scenario, with inflation above 6% next year [2][3].

Governor Andrew Bailey said he understood the arguments for a further hike, before then adopting a more conditional approach, provided the conflict in the Middle East does not ease. The bank does not want this seen as the start of a long series of hikes [2][3].

In the markets, the yield on ten-year UK government bonds rose slightly, to around 5.15%, and the two-year yield to around 4.78%. The pound benefited only briefly from the decision, and the London stock market fell the same day with the slide in US tech [3][5].

Key takeaway: the United Kingdom joins the countries raising rates in the face of energy-driven inflation, like Australia, which did so on Tuesday. It is a sign that the Gulf war is no longer just weighing on oil: it is changing central bank policy [3][5].

The dilemma is well known: raising rates curbs prices, but also credit, investment and jobs. Inflation at 5% erodes purchasing power, but rates at 4% increase repayments for British households, many of whom have an adjustable-rate mortgage [1].

Bailey's message, more nuanced than the number, matters as much as the hike: according to Commerzbank, the next hike could come in February rather than December. Markets are therefore pricing less an automatic series than the path of oil [3].
For UK public finances, higher rates make debt more expensive: the Treasury will pay more for each new borrowing.

If you have ties to the United Kingdom (studies, family, property purchase, travel), the pound and local rates matter. For a reader in France, the decision is above all a signal: the ECB, which makes its announcement on December 17, could also be pushed to raise its rates if eurozone inflation (4% in October) does not fall.

news.2026-11-07-canada-chomage-6-7-pourc: Canada: unemployment rises to 6.7% in October, a six-month high, with 4,700 jobs lost despite 15,000 expected

According to Statistics Canada, the country lost 4,700 jobs in October while economists had expected 15,000 more, and the unemployment rate rose from 6.5% to 6.7%, its highest level in six months. It is the third increase in a row, amid the trade war with the United States [1][2][3].
Canada lost 4,700 jobs in October, according to Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey, published Friday, November 6. The economists' consensus had pointed to a gain of about 15,000 jobs [1][3].
The unemployment rate rose to 6.7%, versus 6.5% in September: it is the third consecutive monthly increase and the highest level in six months [1][2].
Over one year, employment has grown by only 17,000 jobs, or 0.1%. Wholesale and retail trade lost 28,800 jobs over the month [3].
Young people are hardest hit: unemployment among 15-24-year-olds jumped to 13.7% in October. In Quebec, the unemployment rate stands at 5.7% [3].
Canadian media link this weakness to the trade war with the United States, the country's main customer, which is weighing on exports and hiring [2][3].
These figures come about a week after the Bank of Canada raised its key rate to 2.5%, according to the press: the institution thus faces a cooling labor market just as it tightens its policy [3].

Key takeaway: Canada is under two opposing pressures. More expensive energy pushes prices up, which pushes the central bank to raise its rates, while US tariffs hold back exporting companies, which lowers employment [2][3].

Unemployment at 6.7% remains higher than in the United States (4.1% in October). The gap illustrates how an economy highly dependent on a single trading customer absorbs a tariff conflict: export-linked sectors, such as manufacturing, timber or automobiles, are the first exposed.
Youth unemployment at 13.7% is a social warning sign: a young person entering the labor market during a period of weak hiring carries scars on their income for years [3].
Politically, these figures increase the pressure on the Ottawa government to diversify its trade outlets, from the European Union to China, topics of several of our recent news items.

If you have family or plans in Canada (studies, work permit, expatriation), the job market is less promising than a year ago, especially for young people. For a reader in France, it is also an example of what tariffs can do to an exporting country.

Oil loses nearly 13% in a week: Brent falls back below $100 on hopes of a way out of the Hormuz crisis

Brent ended the week around $98 a barrel, down about 13% over five sessions, its biggest weekly drop since mid-April, according to Trading Economics. Markets are betting on diplomacy in the Middle East, but the threat of new US strikes keeps prices very nervous [1][2][3].
On Friday, November 6, a barrel of Brent settled around $98, according to Trading Economics and Prix du baril ($98.16 to $98.32 depending on the source and the contract tracked) [1][2].
The weekly decline reaches about 13%, the largest since mid-April, according to Trading Economics. On Thursday, the price had fallen to its lowest since August 31, according to Reuters [1][3].

Traders are betting on diplomacy: Qatar is circulating a draft agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Tehran says it is ready to reopen it within two days if its conditions are accepted. Brent was still worth $106 on November 2, versus about $70 before the war, according to AFP [4].

The opposite risk remains: Donald Trump said he would soon decide on new strikes, and attacks on tankers continue in the area. Eurasia Group estimates that in case of escalation, Brent could reach $110 to $125 [2][5].
A barrel at $98 is still more than a third above its pre-war level: the drop corrects part of the surge, it does not erase it [4].

Key takeaway: the oil price does not reflect only supply and demand, but above all the probability that the Strait of Hormuz reopens or closes again. Every political statement shifts this bet and therefore the price, hence the size of this week's moves [3][5].

The “geopolitical risk premium” is the part of the price that pays for the danger of a supply disruption. When hope of a deal rises, this premium deflates all at once, and the price falls without a single extra barrel being produced [3].

This easing has knock-on effects: it lightens the energy bill of importing countries like Europe, India or China, eases inflation a little, and therefore the pressure on central banks that have just raised their rates (Australia, United Kingdom) [1].
But a 13% move in one week is also the sign of a fragile market. Prices can rebound just as fast: on October 17, Brent was still touching $110 when Hormuz flared up.

If you drive or heat your home with heating oil, the drop in crude should show up at the pump or on your bill with a delay of a few days to a few weeks, with no guarantee: it depends on the exchange rate and refiners' margins. We are not saying you should fill up now.

How it works: why oil falls when peace is hoped for

Oil is traded on futures contracts: you buy today a barrel deliverable in a few weeks. Its price therefore factors in what traders think will happen, not only what is happening. When passage through a strait like Hormuz is threatened, buyers pay more to be sure of delivery: that is the risk premium. If a deal looks possible, this premium melts away and the price falls, even before tankers set off again. Conversely, a strike or an attack on a ship pushes it back up within minutes. Big banks and funds, which take long or short positions, amplify these moves: when many sell at the same time, the drop accelerates [1][3][5].
Precedents: what oil did after a crisis peak

The invasion of Ukraine and low global stocks push the crude price to its highest level, adjusted for inflation, since 2014; from June 8, prices fall back until the end of the year, as fear of a recession reduces demand [6].
On the last day of 2022, Brent closed at $85, just $7 more than on January 3: the year's surge had been almost entirely erased [6].
Oil falls to its lowest since March, as rising US inflation raises fears of bigger rate hikes and slowing demand [7].

Why a good jobs number makes Wall Street wince: US bond yields are rising

After Friday's jobs report (165,000 jobs created, unemployment at 4.1%), US Treasury yields rose and the stock market ended mixed. A good number for the economy becomes a risk for equities, because it pushes back Fed rate cuts [1][2].
On Friday, November 6, the US economy posted 165,000 jobs created in October versus about 59,000 expected, unemployment at 4.1% and wages up 3.1% over one year [1].
Markets reacted in a mixed way: Treasury yields rose, according to AFP, and the Nasdaq rebounded 1.09% while the Dow Jones fell 0.46% [2].
According to Zonebourse, the probability of a new Fed rate hike in December rose after the report, which weighs on tech stocks, very sensitive to the cost of money [2].
The Nasdaq was coming off its worst session since April 2025 on Thursday (−5.5%): Friday's rebound erases only a small part of that drop [2].
In August 2026, the opposite logic had applied: employers had cut 23,000 jobs, a surprise result that sent stocks higher, as markets saw it as the possible end of rate hikes [3].

Key takeaway: the stock market does not look only at the health of the economy, but above all at the central bank's expected reaction. The stronger employment is, the longer the Fed can keep rates high, and the more expensive equities, whose value depends on future earnings, seem [2].

A bond's yield is the rate the government pays to borrow. When it rises, putting your money in bonds becomes more attractive and stocks less so, especially the priciest ones like tech. It is an old market reflex: “good news, bad news” [2][4].

There is also an effect on the rest of the world: higher US yields draw capital toward the dollar, which weighs on emerging currencies. The Brazilian real fell on Friday to its lowest level of the year against the dollar, with the dollar worth 5.51 reais.
That said, a single report does not change the course: the Fed still has October's inflation, released on November 10, to refine its December decision.

If you have unit-linked life insurance, a PEA (French equity savings plan) or an index fund, these short-term ups and downs should not change your long-term strategy. Borrowing rates, meanwhile, tend to follow the path of yields: if you plan a loan, keep an eye on how they evolve. We are not explaining here what to buy or sell.

How it works: yields, Fed rates and stocks

A government that borrows issues bonds: it commits to repay with interest. The price of these bonds varies every day on the market; when it falls, the yield (the interest relative to the price paid) rises. Investors constantly compare this nearly risk-free yield with the expected gain from stocks. When employment is strong, they expect the central bank to keep its rates high, they sell bonds whose yield rises, and stocks lose relative appeal, especially those whose earnings are far off, like technology. That is why a good economic number can push the stock market down: it is not the economy that is judged bad, but the cost of money that stays high [1][2][4].

A fast-rising yield raises the cost of credit for the whole economy and pushes stocks down [5].

Novo Nordisk raises its forecasts for the third time in 2026, driven by the Wegovy pill, but US price cuts await

On Wednesday, November 4, Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk raised its 2026 forecasts for the third time, after a better-than-expected third quarter: DKK 79.2 billion in sales, DKK 5.6 billion more than expected. Its stock climbed as much as 6% in Copenhagen [1][2][3].

In the third quarter, sales reached DKK 79.2 billion versus DKK 73.6 billion expected by analysts (FactSet). Adjusted operating profit rose 27% to DKK 31.7 billion [1][2].

Wegovy in pill form, launched in the United States, generated DKK 5.39 billion, versus DKK 4.62 billion expected according to Reuters, and reportedly captures about 80% of new oral prescriptions in that country. CEO Mike Doustdar warned that one good quarter was not enough to speak of a lasting recovery: US list prices for Wegovy and Ozempic will fall to $675 from January 1, 2027 [2][3].

Key takeaway: the market does not look only at the quarter's sales, but above all at the company's ability to hold its margins when prices fall. Novo was selling more products, but had been punished in 2025 for cutting its forecasts, a sign that investor confidence is earned quarter after quarter [1][4].

The pill is the strategic stake: it widens the obesity treatment market to patients who refuse injections, and it gives Novo a weapon against its US rival Eli Lilly. But this battle is also fought on prices, which Washington is pushing down [1][2].
The story also plays out in the United States, where obesity treatment prices are at the heart of the political debate: Novo is cutting its list prices there to $675 in January 2027 [2].
Caution is in order: Citi maintains a neutral rating on the stock, and a strong quarter can be followed by a disappointing one if US prices fall faster than volumes grow [2].

If you are a patient in France or know someone on treatment for obesity or diabetes, competition between Novo and Lilly can affect prices and access to treatments, including in Europe, where they are reimbursed differently. How it works: “guidance”, the forecasts the market watches for

A listed company publishes its results every quarter, but also forecasts for the year, the “guidance”. It is this range, more than the past, that moves the stock: a share price reflects future earnings. When management raises its guidance, it signals that its future earnings will be higher than expected, which can push the stock up; when it lowers it, the opposite happens, often abruptly if the stock was already expensive. Analysts compare published figures with their “consensus”, their average of expectations: a result better than the consensus is a “positive surprise” [1][2][4].
The precedent: when Novo cut its forecasts
Novo Nordisk lowers its sales growth forecast to 8-14% from 13-21% in May, and its stock closes down 21.7% at DKK 346.9, despite a higher second quarter [4][5].
Management cited copies of drugs, a slower-than-expected market and competition: the market punishes a loss of confidence more than past figures [4][5].
The same day, Reuters reports that $70 billion in market value was wiped out, and US rival Eli Lilly drops 5% early in the session; management also announces the arrival of Mike Doustdar as CEO [5].

Industrial output rose 0.7% over the month in September, versus stability expected by economists. August's figure was revised from +2% to +1% [1].

According to Euronews, automobile production led the rise, with the pharmaceutical sector rebounding 8% over the month. Construction fell 2.6% and the manufacture of machinery and equipment 6.5%, according to Destatis [3].
Factory orders rose 4.4% in September, slightly less than the 4.6% expected, after plunging 10.1% the previous month [2].
An economist cited by Euronews judges that high energy prices and rising rates remain major risks, while still seeing modest growth in the short term [3].

Key takeaway: German industry, Europe's engine, is holding up better than expected despite expensive energy. But the figures are volatile from one month to the next, and the drop in machinery (6.5%) shows that fragility remains high [1][3].
These data matter for France: German industry producing more generally buys more parts and components from its neighbors.
A German industry in better shape is rather good news for the jobs of French subcontractors, notably in automotive and aerospace. Rate hikes (United Kingdom, Australia) remain the risk going forward.

news.2026-11-07-australie-rba-hausse-tau: Australia: central bank raises its rate to 4.85% on a split 6-to-3 vote, its highest since 2008

On Tuesday, November 3, the Australian central bank (RBA) raised its rate from 4.60% to 4.85%, by 6 votes to 3. It is the fifth hike of the year and the highest level in 18 years, with inflation expected at 4.5% at the end of 2026 [1][2][3].
Six members of the monetary policy board voted for a 0.25-point rise, to 4.85%, and three to leave the rate at 4.60%: the RBA is therefore divided [2][3].

The bank sharply raised its forecasts: inflation is expected to reach 4.5% in the fourth quarter of 2026, versus 3.6% in the previous forecast, and will not return to the upper end of the 2-3% target before the end of 2027 [3].
The RBA cites high and broad-based inflation, as well as the war in the Middle East and the rise in oil, while acknowledging a slowdown: a falling housing market and rising unemployment [1][3].

According to ABC, two further hikes in the first half of 2027 cannot be ruled out; other analysts consider a pause in December possible, with the split vote weakening the idea of another immediate hike [1][2].

Key takeaway: Australia is one of the first advanced economies to tighten policy sharply because of energy, and the United Kingdom followed on Thursday. The oil shock from the Gulf war is pushing central banks to raise their rates, at the risk of slowing their economies [1][3].
For Asia-Pacific, Australian rates matter: the Australian dollar and the prices of exported commodities (iron, coal, gas) serve as a barometer for China and its neighbors.

For a French reader, the direct effect is small, but it is one more signal that the era of rate cuts is over in several countries. If you are planning a stay or studies in Australia, the cost of local credit is climbing.

news.2026-11-07-rdc-fmi-accord-ebola-240: DR Congo: IMF reaches preliminary agreement with a $240 million disbursement to fight Ebola

This week, the International Monetary Fund reached a preliminary agreement with DR Congo, with a planned disbursement of $240 million to deal with the Ebola outbreak, according to the French Treasury's economic service. The IMF also reached an agreement with Burkina Faso on November 4 [1][2].

According to the French Treasury's Central Africa Economic Briefs (week of November 2 to 6, 2026), IMF staff reached a preliminary agreement with DR Congo providing for a $240 million disbursement to fight Ebola [1].
Such a “staff-level” agreement must still be approved by the IMF's executive board before the money is paid out: it is not an immediate payment [1][2].
Separately, the IMF reached a staff-level agreement with Burkina Faso on November 4, 2026 [2].
The outbreak is already weighing on the region: in late October, Uganda imposed a 21-day quarantine, at the travelers' expense, on those returning from DR Congo.

Key takeaway: an epidemic is costly for an already fragile country. Health spending and the drop in trade and travel widen the deficit, and IMF financing helps avoid a debt crisis in the midst of a health emergency [1].
For DR Congo, the world's top cobalt producer, stability also matters for the battery and electronics industries that depend on it.

Congolese cobalt ends up in phone and electric car batteries: a prolonged health crisis could disrupt mines and deliveries, and therefore prices. For a trip to Central Africa, health guidance varies by country.
